rules.exact_quote:
30. So long as the lessee retains the legal possession of the whole of the premises he does not commit a breach of law against parting with the possession by allowing other people to use the same. A tenant cannot be said to part with the possession of any part of the premises unless his agreement with the license wholly ousts him from the legal possession of that part. If there is anything in the nature of a right to concurrent user there is no parting with possession: See Stenina v.
Abrahama, (1931) f Ch D 470 and G. D. Chaudhary v. Anand Sarup. 1966 Delhi Lt 28.
31. Clause (b) of the proviso to cite8†Section 14(1) uses three expressions namely 'sublet', 'assign' and 'otherwise parted with the possession of the whole or any part of the premises without obtaining the consent in writing of the landlord'. These three expressions deal with different concepts and apply to different circumstances.
In subletting there exists the relationship of landlord and tenant as between the tenant and his sub-tenant and all the incidents of letting or tenancy have to be found, namely the transfer of an interest in the estate payment of rent, and the right to possession as against the tenant in respect of the Premises sublet. In assignment the tenant has to divest himself of all the rights that he has as a tenant.
The expression "parted with possession" undoubtedly postulates parting with possession session means giving possession to persons other than those to whom possession has been given by lease and "parting with possession" must have been by the tenant.
The mere user by other persons is no parting with Possession so long as the tenant retains the legal possession himself or in other words there must be vesting of possession by the tenant in another person by divesting himself not only of physical possession but also of the right to possession. The divestment or abandonment of the right to possession is necessary in order to invoke the clause of parting with possession: See cite11†Hazari Lal v. Gian Ram . 1972 Ren Cr 74 (Delhi).
rules.scope: Delhi DRC14(1)(b), distinct sublet/assignment/parting branches; retained legal possession vs mere user
rules.limitations: Doctrine not a universal rule equating company with tenant; actual ouster/control must be checked

rules.exact_quote:
22. If an individual takes the premises on rent and then converts his sole proprietorship concern into a Private limited company in which he has the controlling interest he cannot be evicted from the premises. On the proved facts, this is the inevitable conclusion. The person who took the premises on rent remains in possession though he forms a company and ceases to be the sole proprietor. He does not cease to be in possession. He has not parted with the possession with any one.
He has changed the form of his business. In Interads Vishwa Nath was the sole proprietor. In Interads Private Limited he has the controlling interest and his wife and his two sons are the other shareholders along with two other strangers. He was all in all in his proprietorship concern. Now also he is the chief executive, chairman and the managing director of the company.
It is true that the company is a juristic person but in each case what we have to see is whether Possession has been parted with and whether there is an ouster of the tenant. If the company is a facade concealing the true facts it may be necessary for the Court to pierce the corporate well.
rules.scope: Corporate form versus real loss of possession/control
rules.limitations: Factual illustration of controlling interest, not every company an alter ego; no target-specific conclusion

rule_reviews.reason: The proposal exactly preserves the supplied section 14(1)(b) text, including the post-9 June 1952 timing, the three alternative routes, and the written-consent requirement.

The Delhi High Court excerpt directly supports the proposal's distinctions among subletting, assignment, and other parting with possession. It also directly supports the decisive retained-possession test: mere use by others is insufficient while the tenant retains legal possession, and parting requires vesting possession in another through divestment of physical possession and the right to possession.

The excerpt supports the stated corporate-form qualification: formation or use of a company does not by itself answer the possession question; the inquiry is whether possession was actually parted with and whether the tenant was ousted, with veil-piercing reserved for a facade. The proposal correctly limits the controlling-interest narrative to a factual illustration rather than turning it into a universal alter-ego rule.

condition_reviews.reason: C1 exactly preserves the statutory timing threshold.
C2 correctly identifies subletting as one alternative statutory route with C1 attached by AND.
C3 correctly identifies assignment as a separate alternative statutory route with C1 attached by AND.
C4 correctly identifies other parting with possession as the third alternative statutory route with C1 attached by AND.
C5 correctly attaches the absence of written landlord consent to whichever alternative route applies and preserves the alternatives with OR dependencies.

The source directly supports the proposed subletting qualification requiring incidents of letting or tenancy, including transfer of an interest, payment of rent, and a right to possession against the tenant. C6 confines this proposition to the subletting branch and does not turn it into a target finding.

The source directly supports the parting-with-possession qualification that mere third-party use is insufficient while legal possession is retained, and that divestment of physical possession and the right to possession is required.

The source directly supports treating corporate form as a qualification to the possession inquiry: actual parting with possession and ouster must be examined, and veil-piercing is reserved for a facade. The proposal does not generalize the source's controlling-interest facts into a target conclusion.
